evals.prompt: I run developer marketing at Velmont. We ship a Python SDK and a hosted API. Google Analytics says we had 4,200 docs sessions last month. PyPI says 61,000 downloads. Our CDN logs show about 19,000 unique IPs hitting /docs. My VP wants one headline 'developer reach' number for the board deck next week, and honestly the three numbers being this far apart makes us look like we don't know our own product. Can you reconcile these into something I can present?
evals.expected_output: A refusal to blend the three sources into one reach figure, an explanation of client-side blocking on a developer audience with the published measurement attached, each number labelled with what it actually counts, and a recommendation to move docs collection first-party or proxied.
expectations: States that a third-party client-side analytics script is blocked by roughly 58% of a tech audience, and attaches that figure to a published measurement rather than presenting it as its own estimate.
Names at least one per-segment blocking rate (68.2% desktop, 88.3% Firefox, or 82.3% Linux) when explaining that the miss rate is not uniform.
Refuses to average or blend the client-side session count with the server-side CDN log count into a single figure.
States that the blocking bias varies by page, so it cannot be corrected by applying one multiplier.
Declines to produce a single headline 'developer reach' number spanning the three sources.
Labels each of the three numbers with the source it came from and what that source actually counts.
Recommends first-party or proxied collection on the docs site as the fix that recovers the missing share, rather than switching to a different third-party tool.
Advises trusting ratios inside one source, such as step-to-step drop-off, over absolute counts compared across sources.
States that the PyPI figure is a request count and cannot be converted into a count of people or users.
Reconciles the gap between the sources explicitly instead of splitting the difference.
Does not offer bot traffic or a tracking misconfiguration as the leading explanation for the gap between analytics and the CDN logs.

evals.prompt: Kestrelbase here. Our open-source repo has been going since March and we're putting together a nine-month retrospective for our investors. I want a chart of unique visitors and clones per week since launch, plus top referrers over that whole period. Nobody has exported anything before, we just look at the Insights tab when we remember. Can you tell me how to pull that history, and what else I should be grabbing from the repo while I'm in there?
evals.expected_output: A statement that the nine months of repository traffic history is unrecoverable, a daily snapshot job with owner and schedule, a dated baseline captured today, and the bias warnings on clones, stars and referrers.
expectations: States that the forge's traffic endpoints retain only 14 days of data.
States plainly that the nine months of history requested cannot be recovered and that backfill is impossible.
Instructs scheduling a daily export appended into the team's own store, and explains that a monthly or weekly export loses most of the window.
Notes that traffic endpoint data is readable only for repositories where the caller holds write access.
Warns that clone counts include CI systems and mirrors and are not people.
Warns that stars only ever increase, and recommends converting to stars-per-period if reported at all, never as a headline.
Notes that referrers into a repository are largely stripped, the same way web referrers are.
Names issue or pull-request API signals worth collecting alongside traffic, such as first-time contributor count, time to first response, or external pull requests merged.
Records today's values as a dated baseline before any further instrumentation work.
Does not propose reconstructing the missing traffic history from git history, a third-party mirror, or an archive as an equivalent substitute.
Frames the deliverable as a collection recipe plus a snapshot job with a named owner and schedule, rather than as a traffic analysis.

evals.prompt: Orbitlane. We publish the same client library on npm and on PyPI. Last month npm reported 412,000 downloads and PyPI reported 88,000. We're raising a seed round and the deck has a slide that says '500K developers using Orbitlane'. The investor's associate asked where the number comes from and I need to answer them today. Also our npm number dropped 30% last week and I want to know whether we should be worried.
evals.expected_output: A refusal of the summed developer count, the two registries' counting definitions side by side, a per-registry series against its own baseline, and a first-party alternative for the adoption claim.
expectations: Refuses to present the summed 500,000 figure as a count of developers or users.
States that npm counts HTTP 200 responses serving tarball files, so build servers, mirrors and analysis bots are counted deliberately.
States that PyPI excludes known mirrors by default and exposes with-mirrors and without-mirrors as separate series.
States explicitly that the two registries measure different things and that their figures must never be summed.
Recommends reporting each registry's trend against its own baseline, one series per registry with its counting definition written beside it.
Notes npm's retention limits when planning collection: 18 months of history, 365 days for bulk queries, 7 days per version.
Notes PyPI's 180-day time-series retention and recommends snapshotting into the team's own store.
Mentions the guidance that below roughly 50 downloads per day the npm signal is mostly automation.
Considers CI, mirror or automation behaviour as candidate causes of the 30% drop before drawing any conclusion about adoption.
Does not offer a conversion ratio or divisor for turning downloads into a developer headcount.
Proposes a defensible alternative number grounded in a first-party signal instead of accepting a registry figure as the adoption claim.

evals.prompt: Thornwick AI publishes six models and three datasets on a public model hub. Our board slide currently says '1.2M downloads', which is our model downloads plus our dataset downloads added together. One model has 40,000 downloads and 12 likes; another has 900 downloads and 310 likes, and we've been telling people the second one is our breakout. We also want to start tracking our trending rank weekly, and I'd like to know how many distinct people have pulled each model. We poll the hub API from a cron job without an API token.
evals.expected_output: A rejection of the combined download figure on counting-definition grounds, a correction of the likes-as-adoption reading, trending rejected as a tracked metric, the unique-downloader question declared unanswerable on the free tier, and the untokenized polling job flagged.
expectations: States that a model download on that hub counts every HTTP GET or HEAD against a per-library query file such as config.json, so repeated automated access counts every time.
States that a dataset download collapses every file one IP fetches from one repository inside a 5-minute window into a single download.
Concludes that model and dataset counts are not summable, and rejects the combined 1.2M figure.
States that unique-downloader figures are not available by default and require a paid enterprise add-on, so 'how many people' is unanswerable from the public surface.
Corrects the likes-versus-downloads reading: likes are a recency signal concentrating on new releases while downloads concentrate on older dependencies, and neither proxies the other.
Instructs keeping likes and downloads as two separate series, each labelled with what it means.
Rejects trending rank as a tracked metric because the score has no published formula and no stability guarantee, allowing it only as a snapshot observation.
Flags that the untokenized polling job falls under a lower anonymous rate limit enforced over fixed 5-minute windows, and instructs sending a token.
Warns that a collection job silently returning rate-limit errors produces a flat line that reads as lost adoption.
Instructs snapshotting totals daily into the team's own store and reporting deltas, because the public API returns current totals rather than history.
Does not treat this hub's download counts as comparable to a package registry's download counts.

evals.prompt: Marrowfield Data. Our CEO asked me to put a number in the OKRs: docs visitor to signup conversion rate. I've been reading around and the figure people keep citing for developer tools is 20-40% activation, so I was going to set 25% as our Q3 target and back into how much docs traffic we need to hit it. We've had analytics on the docs for five weeks. Can you help me build the tracking plan that proves we hit it?
evals.expected_output: A refusal of the borrowed target, the activation band named and rejected specifically, target-setting routed to the metrics sibling skill, and a baseline-capture plan built from a decision list offered instead.
expectations: Declines to supply or endorse a docs-conversion or activation target borrowed from other companies.
Identifies the 20-40% activation band as resting on repetition rather than on a measured cohort, and refuses it by name.
States that a healthy conversion rate is a property of one program's own audience and surface mix, so any target must come from the program's own trailing baseline.
Routes the target-setting question to samber/developer-relations-skills@devrel-metrics rather than answering it here.
Offers a baseline-capture plan that would produce a real target, instead of refusing without an alternative.
Starts the plan from a decision list, naming the decisions the data should change and the question that settles each one.
States that an event tracing to no decision on that list is deleted rather than deferred.
Warns that five weeks of client-side docs data on a developer audience is a biased and partial denominator for any conversion rate.
Does not invent a substitute benchmark figure of its own and present it as typical for the category.
Labels any threshold it does propose explicitly as a self-set starting point the user may move.
Declines to frame the deliverable as a plan that proves a pre-chosen number was hit.

evals.prompt: Delacroix Systems. Quarterly review is Thursday. Our join coverage is at 74% and I want to write 'below the industry standard of 80%' in the deck so the web team takes the remediation seriously. It was 89% in June. Our head of data will read this. Is that wording fine, and what should I put next to it?
evals.expected_output: The phrase refused, the 80% identified as a self-set floor, corrected wording supplied, and the writeup redirected onto which surface stopped resolving and when, with an owner and a re-trace.
expectations: Refuses the phrase 'industry standard' applied to the 80% figure.
States that 80% is a floor the plan set for itself, not a published or measured benchmark, and that no such benchmark exists to cite.
Warns that a reader who catches a self-set number dressed as a benchmark discounts the rest of the plan.
Supplies corrected wording that presents the floor as one the team set in its own plan.
Redirects the writeup toward which surface stopped resolving and when, rather than toward the distance from a threshold.
Uses the drop from 89% in June as the comparison that matters, measuring the program against its own past.
Names the identity spine, the anonymous-ID cookie or cross-subdomain sharing as the mechanism to investigate for a coverage drop.
Recommends replacing the 80% floor with the program's own trailing rate once enough of its own data exists.
Attaches a named owner and a re-trace action to the finding.
Explains that join coverage is the preferred standing health check because it is more diagnostic than reconciling absolute counts between two tools.
Does not cite any external company's or vendor's join-coverage figure as a comparison point.

evals.prompt: Palewood. We inherited a tracking plan with about 140 events, all named in Proper Case like 'Docs Page Viewed' and 'Python Quickstart Step 3 Done'. I'm cleaning it up this sprint: converting everything to snake_case, renaming 'Python Quickstart Step 3 Done' to 'quickstart_step_3_completed', and splitting 'Docs Page Viewed' into 'reference_page_viewed', 'guide_page_viewed' and 'blog_page_viewed' so we can query them separately. Sanity-check my plan?
evals.expected_output: The casing conversion advised against on consistency grounds, the per-section split and the baked-in step number rejected in favour of properties, the history-splitting cost of renames stated, and a property registry required.
expectations: Advises against converting the existing plan's casing, and instructs matching the convention already in place.
States that consistency is the sourced rule and that no particular casing is mandated by the naming framework.
Names the Object-Action naming framework as the convention the plan should follow: object then action, past tense.
Warns that renaming a shipped event splits its history in two.
Offers the alternative to renaming: add a property, or version the plan and note the break.
Rejects splitting the page-view event into three per-section events, because that pushes context into the event name.
Instructs carrying the section as a property on one event instead.
Rejects the step number baked into the event name and instructs carrying step_number as a property.
Notes that 140 events is past the readability limit, and that the list should be small enough to fit on one screen.
Requires a property registry giving a type and an allowed-value list per property.
Bans PII and PII-shaped identifiers from every property.

evals.prompt: Hollybrook. Two problems. First, nearly every session in our reports shows the source as our own docs domain. I assumed that was good news until someone pointed out it can't be. We do tag internal docs links with utm_source=docs so we can see which docs pages send people to the pricing page. Second, launch week was 78% 'direct' and our CMO thinks the tracking is broken. We use a link shortener for conference links and everything goes through an OAuth login before signup. Tell me what to fix.
evals.expected_output: Internal tagging named as the cause of the self-referral and stripped, the direct bucket explained as normal with its referrer-stripping causes, the query string checked through shortener and OAuth hops, and a closed tagging vocabulary plus a link register set up.
expectations: Identifies tagging internal links as the cause of the self-referral, and instructs stripping the tags from internal links.
Explains that an internal tag restarts the session and overwrites the real inbound source with the team's own.
Instructs excluding the team's own domains from source classification.
States that a large direct bucket during launch week is the normal case rather than an instrumentation defect.
Names referrer-stripping causes for the direct bucket, such as aggregators, chat clients, privacy browsers, PDFs or slide decks.
Cites that roughly 70% of AI-assistant-driven traffic arrives with no referrer at all.
Warns that shorteners, redirect chains and OAuth hops kill the tag unless they preserve the query string, and instructs verifying that they do.
Answers the internal docs-page question with a first-party mechanism such as an event property or click property, rather than with campaign tags.
Requires a closed allowed-list vocabulary for source and medium, fixed before the next tagged link is published.
Requires every published tagged link to be registered in one table with owner and publish date.
Recommends tagging per artifact rather than per campaign when the point is comparing artifacts.

evals.prompt: Nordvale. We have eight months of signups where the 'channel' field on the record is a mess: about 40% blank, the rest filled in by whoever noticed at the time. I want to run a backfill job so that for every signup we look at which campaign was live that week and write that campaign's channel into the field, making the whole history consistent so the board chart has no gaps. We ran three to five campaigns at a time most months and they mostly landed on /get-started. Then I want to chart the last eight months as a trend.
evals.expected_output: The overwrite refused, the campaign-window heuristic's three pinning conditions stated and found unmet, three source fields required instead of one, backfilled rows kept visually separate, and the eight-month trend chart declined.
expectations: Restricts backfill to records whose source is blank, and forbids overwriting any record already carrying a journey-linked or self-reported value.
Rejects the proposed job specifically because it would overwrite populated rows.
States the three conditions the campaign-window heuristic requires: the date falls inside exactly one campaign's window, the landing page belongs to that campaign, and that campaign's tags were live.
Concludes that three to five concurrent campaigns sharing the /get-started landing page break the pin, so those records must be written as unknown.
Instructs recording three fields rather than a bare channel: source, source_basis and source_confidence.
Defines the source_basis values as journey_linked, self_reported and campaign_window.
States that confidence is judged on the quality of the evidence and is never read off the basis.
States the fail-closed rule: when the merge is ambiguous, record nothing, because a gap is visible and fixable while a wrong merge is corruption nobody later detects.
Requires backfilled history to be kept visually separate so it is not read as a trend.
Declines to present the eight-month backfilled series as a trend chart.
Does not propose a probabilistic or fractional allocation of ambiguous conversions across the concurrent campaigns.

evals.prompt: Cinderbank, series A devtool. I'm the only DevRel person. Board meeting in three weeks and I have to show something about whether our content is working. Engineering will not give me a sprint; best case I get one web-team ticket done in a month, and there's no data team. Right now I have nothing: no analytics on the docs, no tagging, nothing. I own the docs site, the blog, two repos, a Discord, and we publish on npm. Product analytics exist but belong to the product team and they've said no twice. What do I build?
evals.expected_output: An explicitly stated build order by value per hour, the near-zero rungs first, the rungs the constraints rule out deleted from the plan with the deletion written down, and baselines captured on the expiring surfaces before anything else.
expectations: Sequences the work by value returned per hour and states the ranking out loud rather than implying it through row order.
Puts the tagging vocabulary and link registry first, as an hour of decisions requiring no engineering.
Puts snapshot jobs for the expiring surfaces second, justified by history that cannot be bought later.
Puts the self-reported source field at signup third, as near-zero effort.
States that links published before the tagging vocabulary exists stay unmergeable forever.
Deletes the rungs the stated constraints rule out, such as log analysis, product-side events and CLI or SDK telemetry, rather than parking them at the bottom of the list.
Writes the deletion and its reason into the plan document, because a parked rung returns next quarter as unbudgeted scope.
Names what the efficiency order starves, the high-value high-effort work such as the identity spine and product-side events, and states the condition that promotes it anyway.
States that the identity spine is promoted ahead of everything once a decision on the list asks whether a surface produces signups.
Ties the three-week deadline explicitly to promoting the near-zero rungs and deferring the identity spine.
Captures baselines on the expiring surfaces before any other instrumentation work begins.

evals.prompt: Ravenstock. Big week: we shipped cross-domain identity stitching on Monday and attributed signups went from 4 in the previous week to 261 this week. The analytics debugger is green on every event and our tag manager shows everything firing. I'm writing the monthly update. Can you help me frame this as the win it is, and tell me whether there's anything left to check before I hit send?
evals.expected_output: The jump identified as instrumentation rather than growth and annotated, the green debugger rejected as evidence, and an end-to-end trace plus internal-traffic exclusion required before the update goes out.
expectations: States that the jump is instrumentation, not growth, and must be annotated as such before anyone reports it.
Instructs comparing only within the post-stitch period until a full cycle has passed.
Explains that first-party attribution reads near zero until the cross-domain stitch is verified in production, then flips the week it lands.
States that a green debugger proves something is configured, not that anything is measured correctly, and is not evidence.
Requires an end-to-end trace of each primary conversion event, walked as a real user in a fresh browser profile arriving through a tagged external link.
Requires confirming that the landing URL keeps its query string through redirects and OAuth hops.
Requires finding the stored record and confirming the identity fields resolved, with anonymous_id present and user_id attached on the signup event.
Requires finding the row in the report the funnel view will actually read, and names it as the step teams skip.
Requires a duplicate check by refreshing the confirmation page and re-entering through the back button, confirming the deduplication key holds.
Requires excluding internal, office, VPN, CI and preview-deployment traffic, and notes that exclusion filters are not retroactive.
Requires confirming the exclusion filter is active rather than merely defined.

evals.prompt: Quillon. Last quarter we did 19 conference talks and 11 of the people we met later opened an account, so I want to report a 58% talk-to-signup conversion rate. It's our strongest number. I also want to start a public leaderboard in our community server showing the top 20 answerers each month with their handles and answer counts, and set every advocate a target of four published blog posts per month. Does that all hold up?
evals.expected_output: The 58% rate refused on small-N grounds and replaced by a dated raw list, the off-web attribution basis named and framed as a floor, the public leaderboard refused without consent, and the posts target paired with a counter-metric.
expectations: Rejects the 58% rate because it is computed on fewer than roughly 30 events.
Instructs publishing the raw list with dates instead of a percentage at that volume.
Notes that DevRel counts such as talks, enterprise conversations and external pull requests are naturally small, so this is the normal case rather than an exception.
Flags that the talk-to-signup link needs a stated evidence basis, since off-web appearances cannot be tagged.
Names the substitutes for off-web attribution: a short speakable vanity path per talk, a QR code per event resolving to a tagged URL, or a self-reported source field at signup.
States that those substitutes read as a floor on the surface's contribution, never as a total.
Refuses the public per-member leaderboard without consent from the members it would name.
Pairs the four-posts-per-month target with a quality counter-metric, and explains that an incentivised volume metric gets gamed once it becomes a target.
Attributes the gaming dynamic to the published measure-becomes-a-target principle rather than presenting it as an original observation.
Requires person-level community data to be aggregated before anything is published.
Keeps the self-reported source field's answer list short and stable across quarters so periods stay comparable.

evals.prompt: Arbordyne. We sell a platform to enterprises, but individual engineers sign up for the free tier first and then a procurement conversation starts months later. We built account rollup by matching on email domain, and now we have one 'account' holding 4,100 people, plus a long tail of accounts with exactly one person each. Sales wants a report of 'accounts that had a devrel touch before they became an opportunity'. Our CRM has a lead source field and nothing else. What do we fix?
evals.expected_output: Free-mail domains identified as the cause of the giant account and excluded from matching, the one-person accounts diagnosed as unresolved, the resolved share required in any account-level rate, and the influenced-pipeline report gated on whether the CRM can carry an account-level touch record.
expectations: Identifies free-mail domains as the cause of the 4,100-person account, and instructs excluding free-mail-class domains from account matching.
Explains that free-mail domains identify no company, so matching on them collapses strangers into one account.
Diagnoses the one-person accounts as signup domains that never resolved to a company, and recommends enrichment or manual matching as the fallback.
Requires reporting what share of the population actually resolved to an account.
Forbids presenting an account-level rate computed from a partially resolved population without stating that share.
States that in a company-buying motion every event must carry account_id alongside user_id.
Identifies this as the both-at-once motion, instrumenting person-level everywhere and rolling up to account only where an org object genuinely exists.
States that the influenced-pipeline report depends on the CRM being able to carry an account-level touch record, and that a lead source field alone cannot honestly support it.
Settles that dependency before the report is promised to sales, rather than after.
Resolves account_id from the signup domain or the product's own org object, not from a person-level identifier.

evals.prompt: Brightmoor CLI, about 30,000 installs. Leadership wants usage data, and my plan is to turn telemetry on by default in the next minor release, send the full command line the user typed plus the working directory path so we can see what kinds of projects people use it in, hash the machine ID, and mention it in the release notes. We also want a Slack alert per event. How do I position this to the community?
evals.expected_output: The command line and working directory rejected outright, the documented collection floor named, a visible first-run notice and a documented disable path required, and the whole proposal checked against the decision list before it is built.
expectations: Rejects sending the full command line and the working directory path.
States the rule that code, paths and arguments are never sent.
Names the documented floor of what may be collected, such as the command invoked, the tool or framework version, the OS, plugins, and build duration or size.
Requires a visible first-run notice rather than a mention in release notes.
Requires opt-out at minimum, with a documented environment variable or command that disables collection.
Requires documenting exactly what is sent.
States that hashing is not consent.
States that a telemetry surprise costs more community trust than the data returns.
Places CLI or SDK telemetry last in the build order on value per hour, and notes that its cost is paid in community trust rather than in hours.

Names the stricter opt-in model, where uploadable counters are approved through a public proposal process and results are published back openly, as an option that trades reach for trust and carries real governance overhead.
Checks the proposal against the decision list, naming the decision the telemetry would change or cutting it.
